# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
This comment splits into two parts. Sections 1–5 are a valuable, mostly well-executed re-analysis. Sections 6–8 draw a conclusion ("entirely an artifact") that the authors' own numbers, and the Varden trial they cite, don't support.

## What checks out

- **Table 2:** all four rows are correct.
  - 95.1 / 0.8 = +18.9%
  - 98.4 / 0.859 = +14.6%
  - 95.4 / 0.861 = +10.8%
- **Hours ratios:** 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859 and 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861.
- **Revenue:** 1.014 / 1.041 = 0.974, a real fall of 2.6%.
- **"Roughly four points" and "roughly six points":** both match the data (3.8 points on output; 20% vs 14.1% on hours).

## 1. The abstract misdescribes the analysis

- **"Correcting the first three"** includes attrition, but no attrition correction appears anywhere. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. The 10.8% still comes from survivors.
- **Revenue is listed among four problems that "account for most of the reported gain."** Revenue never enters the per-hour calculation, so it can't account for any of the gain.
- **Accurate version:** correcting output and hours in a non-random subset of 17 organisations reduces the gain from 23.4% to 10.8%. Attrition bias is additional and unquantified.

## 2. An internal inconsistency in §3

The time logs reportedly show "+0.7 hours per day" on the four working days, plus 1.6 hours on the day off. That adds 2.8 + 1.6 = 4.4 hours above the 32 scheduled, about 36.4 hours. The reported figure is 34.6.

The numbers reconcile exactly if 0.7 is **per week**: 32 + 0.3 (the baseline excess over 40) + 0.7 + 1.6 = 34.6. This is likely a typo, but it needs fixing because it is the evidence for the central hours correction.

## 3. The sections that work well

**Attrition (§1)** is the strongest new finding. Halden said nine organisations withdrew "during the preparation phase." The microdata show seven withdrew after the reduced schedule began, mostly citing workload. That is a material misstatement in the original paper and deserves prominence.

Two gaps remain:
- The exit reasons sum to 8 of 9; the ninth is unaccounted for.
- The bias is not quantified. Simple bounds would help, such as recomputing the pooled index assuming the nine withdrawers had output of 85, 90 or 95. Lee-style trimming bounds would be better.

**Output measure (§2)** is persuasive in direction: 19 of 23 managers rated output above their own records. But records are not automatically the truth.
- **"Billable hours delivered"** is an input measure. Under a 32-hour schedule it falls mechanically, whatever happens to value per hour. Organisations using it should be excluded, or reported separately.
- **Partial measures** such as tickets closed or units produced may capture less of total output than the manager's judgment does.
- **Weighting:** Halden used employee-weighted means, and the comment doesn't say which weighting it uses.

**Revenue (§4)** is correct. One caveat: CPI is a rough deflator for business revenue, and sector-specific price indices would be better. The conclusion that real revenue likely fell stands either way.

**Sectoral claims (§5)** correctly identifies that any index above 80 registers as a per-hour gain. However, the "fall of 11.2%" in retail rests on **three organisations** and should be presented with that caveat.

## 4. The conclusion contradicts the authors' own data and their main source

**The 10.8% residual is not zero.** After every correction the authors can make, a gain remains. Calling it "entirely an artifact" requires the novelty argument to remove the remaining 10.8%, and §6 is conjecture, not a correction.

**The Varden trial contradicts the conclusion.** The comment treats Varden as "the most reliable finding in the literature," but cites only its counter stratum. Varden's case-processing stratum used exactly the design the comment recommends:
- randomisation;
- record-based output;
- actual hours from timesheets;
- a registered analysis plan.

It found output per actual hour **+12.5% (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4)** at nine months, with no significant loss of output per employee. That is close to the comment's own corrected 10.8%. Citing one half of a randomised trial and ignoring the half that contradicts the thesis is selective.

Varden's result has caveats of its own, notably the question of whether output was capped by demand. But it is the obvious test of "entirely an artifact," and the claim fails it on its face.

**The comment's evidential standards are applied unevenly.**
- §7 dismisses a correlation across seven offices as "precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate."
- §6 builds the case for novelty on two data points of a self-reported energy scale.
- §5 leans on n = 3 retail organisations.

## 5. The novelty argument (§6)

**The extrapolation is wrong even on its own terms.** Energy fell from 0.61 to 0.29 SD between months 3 and 6, about 0.107 SD per month. A linear extension reaches zero at about **month 8.7**, not month 10. A two-point linear extrapolation of a rise-then-fall curve is fragile in any case.

**Energy is not output.** The argument assumes self-reported energy drives the per-hour gain. If the gain comes from removing low-value time, such as meetings, it need not decay when enthusiasm does.

**The direct test is in the data the authors already have.** Halden collected the output index monthly. If novelty drives the gain, output per hour should peak around month 3 and decline by month 6. The comment has the microdata and doesn't report this trajectory. Without it, §6 is speculation.

**"The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter"** is rhetoric. Both a durable effect and a novelty effect are hypotheses, and the data can partly discriminate between them.

## 6. The meetings hypothesis (§7) is misrepresented

- **Timing:** Varden collected the meeting data at managers' request in month six, before the nine-month results existed. "Selected for analysis after the results were known" may overstate how post hoc it was.
- **Varden's own caveats:** Varden already said the analysis was unregistered, rested on seven offices, and "cannot establish a mechanism." It also registered a confirmatory test. The comment presents Varden as asserting a mechanism and omits all of this.
- **Proportionality:** "Should not be cited as a mechanism" goes further than "should be treated as a hypothesis pending the registered test," which is the position Varden actually took.

## 7. Scope

The Data Note correctly says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." The Conclusion then generalises to "the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes," meaning all schemes, from one uncontrolled pilot. The note and the conclusion contradict each other.

The corrected 10.8% also has no confidence interval. With 17 organisations, it should have one, and it will be wide.

## Suggested revisions

1. Fix the abstract: name the corrections actually made, and remove revenue from the explanation of the per-hour gain.
2. Correct "+0.7 hours per day" to the intended figure.
3. Quantify attrition bias with bounds.
4. Report a CI for the 10.8%, and exclude or separate input-based "output" records such as billable hours.
5. Replace the energy extrapolation with the monthly output trajectory from the microdata.
6. Engage with Varden's case-processing result.
7. Rewrite the conclusion. A defensible version would be: "About half of the reported gain is explained by measurement; attrition bias inflates the remainder by an unknown amount; whether the residual ~11% is durable is unresolved, and the randomised evidence is mixed by type of work."

That version would still be a strong and important comment. The current one undermines its best findings by overclaiming.

## Across the three papers

Read together, the evidence currently supports four points:
- Halden's 23.4% is substantially overstated.
- Coverage-bound work loses output under a shorter week.
- In backlog-type work, a per-actual-hour gain of roughly 10–13% appears in both the corrected pilot subset and the randomised trial.
- Whether that gain is durable, and whether it comes from removed low-value time or from rest, is open, and Varden's 24-month follow-up is the natural test.
